title: David of Sassoun
author: Armenian oral epic tradition
short_summary: The third branch of the epic Daredevils of Sassoun tells of David, son of Great Mher, who as a baby is sent to be nursed by the mother of Msra Melik and who grows up to become Sassoun's defender. With his father's Lightning Sword in his hand and riding the horse Kurkik Jalali, he drives off Msra Melik's tax collectors and finally faces Melik himself — his own half-brother — so that Sassoun need never pay tribute again.
extended_summary:
David is the son of Great Mher. His mother dies, and the baby will not take milk, so he is sent to Msr to Ismil Khatun, the mother of Msra Melik — which means David spends his infancy under the same roof as the half-brother he will one day fight. He is then brought back to Sassoun to his uncle, Ohan of the Loud Voice. The boy's strength is enormous: he herds, he hunts, and he has still not learned to measure what he can do.

David finds his father's fenced hunting ground and pulls the fence down so that the animals can live free, and then rebuilds the ruined monastery of Marutha with forty altars. Msra Melik demands tribute from Sassoun and sends Kouz-Badin at the head of his tax collectors; David sends them home empty-handed. When Kouz-Badin comes back with five hundred men and sacks the monastery, David destroys the whole force.

It comes to war — until an old man persuades them that two men should fight instead of two armies. By the agreement Msra Melik strikes first, three times, and cannot hurt David; David strikes once and cuts him in half, and buries the half he can find, because Melik was half Christian. Later David hears wandering singers praising Lady Khandut, rides to Tabriz and marries her in a church, since she turns out to have been secretly Christian. Their son is Mher the Younger. David himself dies by treachery — shot with a poisoned arrow by his own daughter.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the sword David inherits from his father, Great Mher?

options: The Lightning Sword
The Sword of the Sun
The Sword of Sassoun
The Sword of Marutha

questions.explanation: In Armenian it is Tur Ketsaki, the lightning sword. In this epic weapon and horse pass down by blood and choose their owner: neither Msra Melik nor anyone else can use them — only one descended from Mher.

questions.prompt: Why is the newborn David sent to Msr, to Msra Melik's mother Ismil Khatun?

options: His mother has died and the baby will not take milk
There is famine in Sassoun and the child is saved
Msra Melik has demanded a hostage from Sassoun
His uncle is afraid of the strength in the child

questions.explanation: So David spends his infancy in the very house he will later fight, and Msra Melik turns out to be not merely an enemy but a half-brother. The whole conflict of the epic is born inside one family.

questions.prompt: David finds his father's fenced hunting ground. What does he do with it?

options: Pulls the fence down so the animals go free
Keeps it and hunts there every single day
Gives the ground to his uncle Ohan
Burns the forest so no enemy can hide in it

questions.explanation: The father kept animals penned for his own pleasure; the son lets them out. David inherits his father's strength and weapons but not his habits, and the epic marks this as the first act that is properly David's own.

questions.prompt: What does David raise up out of its ruins in Sassoun?

options: The monastery of Marutha, with forty altars
His father's fortress, with forty stone towers
The bridge of Sassoun, with its forty arches
The old canal, with forty springs

questions.explanation: Rebuilding the monastery is not a stray episode: immediately afterwards Msra Melik's collectors come and sack it, and that is what carries David into war. In this epic the defence of Sassoun begins not with weapons but with building.

questions.prompt: Put the events of David's life in the order they happen.

items: The infant David is sent to Msr to be nursed
He is brought back to Sassoun, to his uncle Ohan
David rebuilds the monastery of Marutha
He sends Kouz-Badin home with empty hands
David meets Msra Melik in single combat

questions.explanation: Notice that the marriage comes after the duel. The epic finishes the public business first — Sassoun is freed from tribute — and only then allows David a life of his own.

questions.prompt: Match each name from the epic to its role.

right: The uncle who raises the boy brought back to Sassoun
The half-brother who demands tribute from Sassoun
The horse that speaks in a human voice
The lady of Tabriz who was secretly a Christian

questions.explanation: The four of them are the four sides of David's life: family, enemy, weapon and love. Note that the enemy is a relative and the horse talks — nobody in this epic is merely scenery.

questions.prompt: Sort each event by when it happens in relation to the duel.

content.groupA: Before the duel with Msra Melik

options.label: The baby is nursed by Ismil Khatun
A monastery is rebuilt with forty altars
The tax collectors go home with nothing
A wedding takes place in a church in Tabriz

questions.explanation: The duel is the middle of the branch, not the end of it. Before it David defends Sassoun; after it he lives his own life — and it is in that second half that the one thing weapons cannot stop reaches him: betrayal.

questions.prompt: An old man persuades David and Msra Melik to fight each other instead of sending in two armies. How does the duel go?

options: Melik strikes three times, then David strikes once
They strike by turns until one of them goes down
David strikes first and wins immediately
They charge each other on horseback three times

questions.explanation: By the agreement the first blow belongs to Melik, and he strikes three times without harming David. David strikes once and cuts him in half, then buries the half he can find, because Melik was half Christian.

questions.prompt: David lets his enemy strike first — three times — although he could have struck first and ended it at once. Was that courage or recklessness? Give your reasons.
questions.explanation: Both positions can earn full marks. A strong 'courage' answer notices that the epic makes David a hero precisely for his fairness, and that Sassoun wins by an honest fight rather than a trick. A strong 'recklessness' answer notices that he was risking the freedom of all Sassoun for the sake of his own honour. Accept either, argued from the epic.

questions.prompt: For centuries this epic was not read but told and sung from memory. Imagine you are the teller and you have time for only one episode. Which would you choose, and why is that the one that should reach the next generation?
questions.explanation: There is no single right answer. A strong answer picks a specific episode — the hunting ground, the monastery, the tax collectors, the duel — and explains what it teaches or why it matters, rather than only saying that it is exciting.

questions.prompt: David's horse is no ordinary horse: it speaks in a human voice, and its name is Kurkik ___.
questions.explanation: Kurkik Jalali is also inherited from Great Mher. In this epic the horse is an adviser rather than transport: he warns David, argues with him, and more than once saves him from his own recklessness.

questions.prompt: How does David die, after being unbeaten in every battle?

options: Shot with a poisoned arrow by his own daughter
In a fresh duel with Msra Melik's brother
In the mountains, caught by snow on a winter march
On a collapsing bridge on the road back from Tabriz

questions.explanation: He is killed not by an army but by treachery from inside his own family. The epic ends the branch this way on purpose: David could not be beaten in open country, so he is killed from hiding, and the whole branch closes on the thought that strength does not protect you from everything.
